statement: Guard against overly complex solutions during design, because excessive system complexity directly limits the ability to scale.
Overengineering takes two forms — exceeding the useful requirements of a product, and making a product overly complex — and the complexity form is the larger threat to scalability.

Test a design for excess complexity by having the engineer present it to engineering peers of varying experience; if any group cannot understand and re-explain it unassisted, treat the design as too complex.

A system can be overly complex in three ways: making the system work harder than necessary, making the user work harder than necessary, or making engineers work harder than necessary to understand it.
Do not build features that only a small fraction of users want.
condition: a feature is wanted by only a small fraction of the user base

statement: Simple, easy-to-understand systems are cheaper to maintain, faster to troubleshoot and restore, and let less-senior engineers contribute, which increases organizational scalability.
Apply the Design-Implement-Deploy (D-I-D) process: design for 20x capacity, implement (code) for 3x capacity, and deploy for roughly 1.5x capacity.
Designing and discussing how to scale is far cheaper than implementing it, so scale design (targeting 20x to infinite) should happen early and frequently at low engineering and asset cost.
In the implement phase, narrow the scale target to roughly 3x-20x current size and code the change about a month before the capacity is needed.
Deploy capacity just-in-time (days before demand) to avoid idle assets diluting shareholder value; keep roughly 1.5x peak for moderate growth and up to ~5x peak for hyper-growth.
condition: moderate-growth versus hyper-growth company

statement: Use the cloud for burst capacity rather than holding idle owned hardware for sudden demand.
Scale is elastic — capacity needs contract as well as expand — so solutions should be designed to flex in both directions.
Simplify a solution in three places: its scope, its design, and its implementation.
Simplify scope with the Pareto (80/20) principle: deliver the roughly 20% of features that produce ~80% of the value and cut the rest.
Cutting unnecessary features reduces dependencies between functions, which makes the system scale more effectively and cost-effectively.

Simplify implementation by reusing proven work: prefer widely-adopted open-source or third-party solutions, then an internally proven solution, then a legally-copyable external approach, and build your own only as a last resort.
The simplest implementation is usually one that has already been built and proven scalable.
Reduce the number of DNS lookups required to download a page, balanced against the browser's limit on simultaneous connections.
condition: web pages where performance matters

statement: Every distinct domain that serves page objects requires a DNS lookup (from cache or a name server), which can cost up to hundreds of milliseconds.
Reduce the number of objects on a page, since object count drives page download time, balanced against maximizing simultaneous connections.
condition: web pages where performance matters

statement: Browsers cap the number of simultaneous persistent connections per domain (HTTP/1.1 specifies 2; many browsers now use 6 or more).
Serve objects across multiple subdomains to exceed the per-domain connection cap and download more objects in parallel.
An online-magazine client cut average page load from about 11 seconds to under 5 seconds by serving objects across seven subdomains.
Combine similar objects (e.g., CSS sprites) to cut request count, but do not over-combine, since one very large object blocks rendering until fully downloaded and wastes parallel connections.
exception: combining produces a single very large object that blocks rendering

statement: The reliable way to find the right object and subdomain balance is to test pages across multiple browsers and connection speeds.
Google reported that adding 400 ms of search latency reduced its daily searches by almost 0.6%.
Do not mix different vendors' switches and routers; standardize routing and switching gear on a single provider.
Heterogeneous routers and switches cause intermittent interoperability and availability problems because vendors implement standards differently and add proprietary protocols.
The single-vendor rule applies only to gear that must communicate to route traffic; for firewalls, load balancers, IDS, and DDoS appliances, choose best-of-breed.
exception: non-routing network gear such as firewalls, load balancers, and IDS

statement: Dividing work across more workers increases throughput (work per unit time) and therefore scalability.
The AKF Scale Cube defines three axes of scaling: X (horizontal duplication/cloning), Y (split by function, service, or resource), and Z (split by customer or lookup).
X-axis scaling clones services and databases behind a load balancer to spread transaction load.
Apply X-axis cloning when the read-to-write ratio is high (5:1 or greater) or when transaction growth exceeds data growth.
condition: read:write ratio >= 5:1 or transaction growth exceeds data growth

statement: X-axis cloning scales transaction volume but not data volume, because it duplicates data and functionality.
The database or persistent-storage tier is almost always the hardest part of a system to scale.
When cloning databases, the accessing code must distinguish reads from writes so reads can be routed to replicas.
Most applications perform far more reads than writes, so creating read-only replicas scales read load effectively.
Keeping replicas perfectly in sync is very costly and often does not return the expected value, so tolerate bounded replication lag where the business allows it.
condition: the business can tolerate slightly stale read data

statement: A reservation client with a 400:1 read-to-write ratio tolerated roughly 90 seconds of replication lag, producing only about 0.1% booking collisions, which were handled by a final check at purchase.
Putting an object cache (a key-value store) in front of the database is a recommended first step before introducing replication.
Y-axis scaling splits a system by function, service, or resource, using verbs (services) and nouns (resources).
Use Y-axis splits for very large data sets where relations are unnecessary, or for large complex systems that need engineering specialization.
condition: large data sets without needed relations, or systems needing engineering specialization

statement: Y-axis splits scale transactions and large data sets and help with fault isolation.
Separating distinct functions' data raises cache hit ratios, which speeds responses and improves resource utilization.
Y-axis splits let large engineering teams specialize in subsets of the system.
Z-axis scaling partitions one data set or service into pieces (sharding/podding), usually by a customer attribute such as customer ID, geography, device, or a modulus/hash.
Use Z-axis splits for very large similar data sets and fast-growing customer bases, or to fault-isolate groups of customers.
condition: rapidly growing similar data sets or need for customer fault isolation

statement: Make shards unequal-sized to limit rollout risk: release first to a small customer segment, then to progressively larger segments.
In hyper-growth, design to scale out (horizontally, by segmenting workloads) rather than up, because scaling up eventually fails.
Scaling up eventually hits a ceiling — either uneconomical cost or no larger machine exists — and also fails on logical contention that bigger hardware cannot solve.
The cost of scaling up rises disproportionately (a power law) relative to processing power gained, while the engineering cost to scale out rises roughly linearly.
Use the AKF Scale Cube to choose the split; horizontal duplication (cloning) is usually the easiest to implement.
Do not rely on Moore's Law to scale a hyper-growth system, since growth can outpace transistor doubling.
Prefer many small, inexpensive commodity systems over a few large high-end systems in production during hyper-growth.
Per-CPU efficiency falls as CPUs are added to a single machine (scheduling, memory-bus contention, hazards), so large machines cost more per CPU yet do less work per CPU.

Compute total cost of ownership (power, space, and cost against an independent utilization benchmark) yourself rather than trusting the vendor; the largest available system almost never wins that math.
Virtualizing one large machine into N domains never yields more total throughput than N equivalent separate systems, because the hypervisor consumes CPU cycles.
Commodity systems allow more redundancy, are cheaper to discard and replace, and fail less often per unit because they have fewer parts.
Design for three or more live data centers to lower overall cost, increase availability, and provide disaster recovery.
A three-site live/live/live configuration needs only about 150% of non-database capacity per overall need and roughly 166% total cost, versus 200% for a two-site hot/cold configuration.
Database storage still requires about 200% capacity regardless of the data-center configuration.
Use the idle capacity of a multiple-live-site design for test zones and to absorb demand spikes.
In a fully connected set of sites, each new site (N+1) adds N network interconnects, so network transit cost grows quickly as sites are added.
Spreading across multiple live data centers requires statelessness (or designed-around state) plus Y/Z fault-isolation and X replication.
condition: moving to a multiple-live-site architecture

statement: Leverage a third-party cloud for temporary, spiky, or inconsistent demand when response time is not a core requirement.
condition: demand is temporary/spiky/inconsistent and response time is not core

statement: Cloud hardware provisions in minutes, versus days or weeks for owned physical servers.
A cloud server's pay-per-use cost breaks even against buying a physical server at roughly 12 months of continuous (24/7) use, so part-time use stays cheaper.
condition: the server is used only part of the day

statement: Use a relational database only when you need ACID transactional integrity or relationships between data; otherwise choose a more appropriate storage tool.
condition: the data needs ACID integrity or relationships

statement: An RDBMS provides transactional integrity and relational structure but is harder to scale, costs more, and has lower availability than many alternative stores.
Data relationships drive flexibility but also raise cost and limit scalability, making the degree of relationships a deliberate scalability tradeoff.
Choose a storage tool by the data's characteristics: degree of relationships, rate of growth, read-to-write ratio, and how well the data monetizes.
Match storage to data: write-once-read-many data (e.g., images) fits a file system, relationship-light non-transactional data fits NoSQL, and large distributed processing fits MapReduce/Hadoop.
NoSQL stores limit inter-entity relationships, which is what lets them distribute across nodes for scale, typically with eventual consistency.
Use firewalls only where they meaningfully reduce risk; treat firewall placement as a business risk-versus-cost decision rather than an all-or-nothing default.
Firewall high-value targets such as PII and PCI data, and do not firewall low-value static content.
condition: content has high value to an attacker
exception: low-value static content such as CSS, images, and JavaScript

statement: Failed firewalls are the second-largest driver of site downtime after failed databases, and firewalls add a scalability chokepoint, an availability risk, and capital cost.
Actively use application log files: aggregate them, monitor them with automated tools, and assign resources to fix the issues they reveal.
Aggregate logs over an out-of-band network and log asynchronously, and archive or purge logs as their value declines, to limit logging's cost to transaction response time.
Never read data back immediately after writing it solely to validate the write; instead act on the error codes returned by the write operation.
Reading after writing doubles the work and roughly halves throughput, and it rarely returns risk-mitigation value commensurate with that cost.
If just-written data will be needed again soon, keep it locally or in cache rather than re-fetching it.
When a regulatory rule appears to require read-after-write verification, perform it asynchronously and never block the user on a synchronous write to two data sources.
condition: a genuine regulatory or legal verification requirement exists

statement: Avoid redirects where possible, because they delay the user, consume computational resources, and are error-prone (e.g., redirect loops).

When a redirect is necessary, prefer a server-configuration redirect (e.g., Apache mod_alias/mod_rewrite in httpd.conf rather than .htaccess) over HTML or code, and return the correct HTTP 3xx status code.
condition: a redirect is genuinely necessary

statement: Relax temporal constraints (such as holding an item's availability from view through purchase) wherever possible, because they are hard to scale under RDBMS consistency.
The CAP theorem states that a distributed system cannot simultaneously guarantee consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.
Adopt a BASE (basically available, soft-state, eventually consistent) approach by relaxing ACID consistency to scale, locking an item at cart/write time on the master rather than on view.
Use a CDN to offload site traffic onto edge servers that hold cached content and route each request to the optimal node.
A CDN reduces required servers, power, bandwidth, and staff and improves availability and response time, at a premium over raw peering cost, so its adoption should be cost-justified and monitored.
Even dynamic pages contain cacheable static content (images, CSS, JavaScript), and CDNs increasingly support dynamic content via mechanisms such as Edge Side Includes.
Control caching with HTTP headers, not HTML meta tags, because many browsers and proxy caches ignore meta tags.
Set Expires and Cache-Control headers per object type, noting that max-age overrides Expires when both are present.
Enable HTTP keep-alives (persistent connections), which Apache reports cut latency by about 50%, balanced against tying up server threads with long timeouts.
Cache Ajax responses with appropriate Cache-Control, Expires, and Last-Modified headers, preferring public and avoiding no-store where the data is not private.
condition: the Ajax data is not real-time-critical and not private

statement: Use stable item IDs rather than relative offsets (such as page/item) in cacheable requests, to avoid coherency and consistency problems.
Per-keystroke Ajax search requests can multiply backend load several-fold, so cache or throttle them.
Deploy a page cache (reverse proxy) in front of web servers to offload requests; the benefit is largest for dynamic content.
Use ETag entity tags to support If-None-Match conditional GETs and maximize cacheability across proxy caches.
Application-level caching is required to scale cost-effectively and must be designed from a systems-architecture perspective.
Iteratively apply the Pareto principle and AKF cube splits (Y and Z) to observed production traffic to maximize cache hit rates.
Object caches are in-memory stores of hashed items used to cache expensive query results or computations, usually placed between the application and database tiers.
Use a Top SQL report (the most frequent and most resource-intensive queries) to decide which queries to eliminate through object caching.
Use a proven open-source or commercial object cache rather than building your own.
Monitor object-cache hit ratio, target roughly 85% or better, and add cache servers when it drops.
Put object caches on their own tier for better memory and CPU utilization and independent scaling, since they need much memory but little CPU.
Learn aggressively from both customers and operations; the organizations that learn fastest grow fastest and scale best.
Learn from customers by launching quickly and watching behavior (usage tracking and A/B testing) rather than trusting stated preferences.
Run a postmortem on every incident to reach the real root cause; mistakes are unavoidable, but repeating the same mistake is unacceptable.
You cannot test quality into a system; testing identifies defects but does not add quality.
Use QA to lower cost, increase engineering velocity and throughput, and raise defect detection, not to create quality.
Hire a QA person when doing so recovers at least one engineer's worth of productivity, typically at lower per-head cost than an engineer.
condition: hiring QA recovers >= one engineer's worth of productivity

statement: In hyper-growth hiring, QA's key value is teaching the organization which recurring mistakes it makes so they can be eliminated.
Always design code so it can be rolled back; failing to design for rollback is designing for failure.
Make database changes additive only: add columns and tables, and do not drop them until a later release deprecates the dependency.
Script and test all DDL/DML changes ahead of time, including the rollback script, and test the rollback under load in staging or QA.
Do not change the semantic meaning of existing data within a release; first release code that handles a new value, then release code that uses it.
Add a wire-on/wire-off (feature-flag) framework, controllable by role and by random percentage, to beta-test features and to disable a faulty feature without a full rollback.
Run a structured postmortem in three phases: build the event timeline, identify issues, then assign SMART actions, each with a single owner.
Address people, process, and technology in every postmortem; no single component failure is the true root cause, so ask 'why' about five times.
For systems that fail rarely, practice mindfulness (preoccupation with failure, reluctance to simplify, sensitivity to operations, commitment to resilience, deference to expertise) to keep learning.
Plan the data model carefully up front, because fixing a broken data model after implementation can cost roughly 100x what it costs during design.
Data relationships determine how a database can be split or sharded, so heavy relationships make later splits difficult.
Higher normal forms add relationships, so to increase scale teams often reduce normal form, trading data integrity for scalability.
For a slow join query, in order: tune the query, use a view/materialized view/summary table, join in the application tier, or push back on the business requirement.
Have a competent DBA review new queries for performance before they reach production.
Database lock granularity is a throughput tradeoff: finer (row) locks raise concurrency but cost more to acquire, while coarser (page or table) locks block more rows.
Let the database optimizer choose lock granularity initially, then monitor production and force a specific lock type where the optimizer is wrong.
Choose a database and storage engine that support multiple lock types and granularities to maximize concurrency; engines limited to table-level locking (e.g., MyISAM) cap throughput.
Reduce lock contention by splitting along the X, Y, or Z axes (read replicas, table separation, or customer partitioning).
Do not use multiphase commit protocols (2PC/3PC); they are blocking and hold app-server threads and database rows until every cohort commits.
Do not use multiphase commits to extend a monolithic database's life; split the data with Y or Z axes instead.
In one deployment, routing under 2% of calls through two-phase commit locked up the site at under a quarter of its previous transaction throughput.
Minimize SELECT ... FOR UPDATE cursors, because they hold row locks until commit or rollback and can stack pending transactions into near-deadlock.
The ANSI SQL standard defaults cursors to FOR UPDATE unless FOR READ ONLY is declared, so use read-only and NOWAIT options to minimize locks.
Never use SELECT * (or INSERT without an explicit column list); always name the columns.
SELECT * and unnamed INSERT break when table structure changes (column remapping), transfer unneeded data, and prevent rollback.
Design fault-isolative swimlanes, where a swimlane is a fault-isolation domain in which a component failure does not affect components in other swimlanes.
Swimlane principle: share nothing — databases and servers are never shared across swimlanes, though some border network gear may be.
Swimlane principle: no synchronous calls cross swimlane boundaries.
Swimlane principle: limit asynchronous calls across swimlane boundaries, since they can still propagate failure.
Swimlane principle: when an asynchronous cross-swimlane call is necessary, implement it with timeouts and wire-on/wire-off control.
condition: an asynchronous cross-swimlane call is necessary

statement: Build swimlanes along the Y or Z axis; they improve availability, incident detection, scalability, cost, and time-to-market.
To keep fault isolation when a swimlane needs a shared synchronous service, duplicate the service per swimlane (e.g., one payment gateway per swimlane) or use a per-swimlane read replica or cache.
condition: a swimlane needs a normally-shared synchronous service or data source

statement: Keep swimlanes on physical-server boundaries; do not mix virtual servers from different swimlanes on one physical host.
Never trust single points of failure; identify and eliminate them, because everything fails.
The database is the most common single point of failure because it is the hardest tier to scale across nodes.
Strive for active/active configurations rather than active/passive to maximize availability.
Quick SPOF mitigations include active/passive failover, master-slave with read/write routing, and load-balancer session affinity, but the best fix is code that runs on many hosts.
Avoid connecting components in series, because components in series have a multiplicative effect on the risk of failure.
Each additional component in series at 99.9% availability adds roughly 43 minutes of downtime per month.
Add parallel redundancy for series components, paying special attention to the database and network/firewall layers that teams commonly overlook.
Build a wire-on/wire-off framework to enable and disable product features for graceful failure.
Implement wire-on/wire-off where implementation cost is less than the risk-weighted cost of failure, applying it to shared or heavily-used services and risky new features rather than everything.
condition: implementation cost is less than likelihood-times-impact of failure

statement: Strive for statelessness, because state and session limit scalability and increase cost by reducing how many users (tenancy) a server can hold.
Always push back on the need for state and justify it with A/B or business metrics; state distribution to a browser or state server is not the same as being stateless.
exception: genuine state-machine or workflow systems that require state

statement: Simple and easy often beats rich and complex, as when Craigslist's largely stateless classifieds beat eBay's feature-rich product and Google's lean search beat richer rivals.
If state is required, first store session data in the user's browser via cookies, so any web server in the pool can serve the request.
condition: state is required

statement: Keep browser cookies small because they are sent on every request, and protect session cookies against sidejacking (e.g., an HTTPS authorization cookie), since unsecured cookies can be captured.
If state cannot live in the browser, use a distributed cache: avoid server affinity, avoid session replication, and locate the cache off the working server on its own tier.
condition: state is required and cannot be pushed to the browser

statement: Do not build your own session cache; choose by persistence versus cost — a database for durability, an object cache for cheap non-persistent speed, or a hybrid.
Favor asynchronous communication over synchronous as much as possible, and design the application to actually behave asynchronously.
Synchronous calls couple services and tiers and cause cascading failures, with a multiplicative effect on both availability and bug risk.
Make calls asynchronous when they go to external/third-party APIs, are long-running, are error-prone or frequently changed, or have no temporal constraint (fire-and-forget).
Calls that must remain synchronous require timeouts and exception handling so failures are handled gracefully.
Scale the message bus like any other critical component, because it is a common single point of failure and is not immune to demand just because it is asynchronous.

Scale a message bus with the Y axis (by service, message attribute, quality of service, resource, or temporal need) and the Z axis (by customer); X-axis cloning works poorly for buses because of reader congestion.
Keep message-bus scaling consistent with the overall architecture; when both Y and Z apply, prefer Z for fault isolation, with a dedicated bus per swimlane.
condition: both Y-axis and Z-axis splits are available

statement: Do not publish everything on the message bus, because the cost of handling a message is roughly constant while data value varies.
Publish high-value data, sample low-cost data, and do not publish low-value/high-cost data; sampling cuts cost while often retaining the data's value.
Scale your own system; do not rely on vendor or proprietary features (such as database clustering) to achieve scalability.
Avoiding vendor scaling solutions protects three things: control of your own destiny, architectural simplicity, and total cost of ownership by avoiding lock-in.
Use vendors for non-core capabilities, but keep scaling itself as your own core competency.
Match storage cost to data value using recency-frequency-monetization (RFM) analysis, and purge data worth less than its storage cost.
Tier storage by value (fast and expensive for high-value data; cheap, archived, or purged for low-value) and treat it as an ongoing process, because data value changes over time.
condition: regulatory or legal retention rules permit purging

statement: Storage is never free — it costs purchase price, occupied space, and power/cooling — so do not assume cheaper storage is free.
Remove business and product intelligence from transaction processing by taking stored procedures out of the database and into application logic.
Do not make synchronous calls between corporate systems (ERP/BI) and the product; move data between them asynchronously via ETL or a message bus.
Keep like transactions together and dedicate expensive databases to relational transactions, so each system can scale independently at the lowest cost.
Adopt 'design to be monitored' as an architectural principle, building hooks (e.g., async timestamps before and after transactions) to record transaction timing.
Monitor first from business metrics to answer 'Is there a problem?', then application monitoring for 'Where?', then system tools for 'What?'.
Detect problems by comparing business metrics week-over-week and alerting on statistical deviation, because high CPU or memory alone does not mean customers are affected.
Be competent in, or buy competency for, every component of your architecture, because to the customer every problem is yours since you deliver a service, not software.
Build-versus-buy and core-versus-context decisions do not excuse incompetence; you must still be able to operate and troubleshoot what you buy.
Larger teams and more-relied-on components warrant in-house expertise, while smaller or less-critical components can be outsourced to partners who have 'skin in the game'.
condition: component criticality and team size

statement: Prioritize scalability work by risk reduction minus cost (R - C = P), where risk equals probability times impact and risk reduction is treated as the benefit.
Measure availability by actual revenue impact rather than wall-clock time, because traffic and revenue are not evenly distributed across the day.
Building these scalability rules in from scratch is much cheaper than retrofitting them into an existing system, for equivalent benefit.
Codify a chosen subset of the rules as architectural principles and enforce them as exit criteria in design and architecture reviews.

For re-architecting an existing platform, the highest-priority (Very High) rules are: relax temporal constraints, use object caches, design for rollback, learn from failures, use the right database lock, do not SELECT everything, be wary of scaling through third parties, and be competent.
Scalability and performance are distinct properties: a solution can be fast without being scalable, and scalable without being fast.
Horizontal scalability — increasing capacity by adding more of the same hardware or software — is the preferred and only genuinely true form of scalability.
Being horizontally scalable is not by itself sufficient; such a system still requires careful engineering to be safe and correct.
Use vertical scaling (adding CPU, RAM, or storage to a single machine) only for problems that are genuinely hard to scale horizontally.
condition: the problem has no legitimate horizontally-scalable solution available on the market

statement: 'Difficult to scale horizontally' means academically difficult (no legitimate market solution), not merely inconvenient.
Large ACID-compliant databases are a class of problem that is hard to scale horizontally, and doing so requires substantial compromise.
Services such as DNS, FTP, and static web content are inherently horizontally scalable and well understood.
exception: building them is still not idiot-proof and demands care

statement: Design for scalability from the beginning for the components that will need to scale, rather than retrofitting scalability later.
condition: for the parts of the system that actually need to scale

statement: Size the system for current demand but architect it so that growth to far larger scale needs no application or architectural redesign.
Provisioning capacity far beyond current demand (building for millions while serving thousands) wastes money.
Account for scaling down as well as up: an application that cannot run on a smaller architecture traps the business in high operating costs when demand falls.
Two companies collapsed because their applications could not scale down — at roughly 10% of original traffic they achieved only about a 20% reduction in operating costs.
Scaling an architecture up is harder than scaling it down, because over-utilization has glaring usability effects while under-utilization has only subtle financial effects.
Adding independent components to an architecture increases its complexity linearly, but adding components that other components depend on increases complexity exponentially.
Scaling any system guarantees four costs: capital investment, increased complexity, higher maintenance costs, and time to act.

The dominant scaling constraint shifts by business type: dotcoms and SMBs minimize up-front investment and time-to-implement, while large firms minimize risk by maximizing simplicity and maintainability.
Build architectures from autonomous, independently and cost-effectively scalable components so a demand increase can be met by scaling only the one or two stressed components.
An architecture of efficient, maintainable components scales better than an efficient, maintainable monolithic architecture.
Anticipating change — forecasting future architectural requirements from business goals, competition, and market — is the defining skill of a good Internet architect.
Scaling is a balance among cost, complexity, maintainability, and implementation latency, with no universally correct proportion.
No programming language inherently scales or fails to scale — solutions scale, not languages — so focus on the nature of the solution rather than the implementation language.
Monitor both technical metrics (are the servers up?) and business-level metrics (is the business functioning?), not just one of the two.
Include the operations group in business and technical development meetings, because development's closeness to the business otherwise loses operations' insights.
Developers will push code to production to meet urgent business demands without regard for stability, repeatedly risking outages.
Adopt an explicit set of failure-avoidance principles and procedures, beginning with educating development and operations teams on the ramifications of failure.

Large systems are run by teams for three reasons: the work exceeds one person's capacity, deep focused expertise is cheaper to hire than broad expertise, and the key-man (bus-factor) risk demands business continuity.
Prefer commodity (current- or prior-generation) hardware over the fastest, biggest hardware for better ROI, because top-of-curve performance costs disproportionately and is rapidly obsoleted.
exception: except for problems that genuinely require premium components

statement: Scale out, not up: buying a large monolithic machine to scale will saturate its capacity and force a costly lesson in the difference between scalability and performance.
Uncontrolled change is a leading cause of architecture failure and shows up as feature creep, milestone hopping, sloppy version control, and premature implementation.
Treat infrastructure as a means to a business goal and actively resist uncontrolled change with disciplined tools and process.
Use version control for everything as the baseline failure-avoidance practice — it is the highest-value, lowest-effort control for rapid development.
A 'push' is any controlled, planned change to the production architecture — code, database schema, vendor upgrades, OS patches, hardware, or network changes.
A complete push plan has four parts: a plan to go from A to B, a rollback plan from B to A, a bare-metal restore plan for A, and a successful test of the forward and rollback plans.
Always prepare and test a back-out plan before a change; in rapid-development environments a tested rollback is fundamental, not optional.
condition: rapid-development environment

statement: Adopt unit testing to catch breakage introduced by rapid changes, even though it is higher-effort than version control and planning.
Testing only verifies expected output for the inputs you supply; no form of testing can ever prove a system works under every possible condition.
Unit-test the whole system, not just parts: a handful of tests across a few of many modules buys little and gives a false sense of confidence.
condition: value rises sharply with completeness of coverage

statement: Do not argue over which version-control system is best; rank the features that matter for your architecture, and consult the VCS's user community about architectures similar to yours.
Open-source version control is sufficient for managing code and configuration, so avoid vendor bias when selecting a VCS.
exception: commercial VCS still helps for proprietary binary formats such as Word documents

statement: A version-control commit must be atomic — either fully succeed or behave as if it never happened — and the VCS must support clean, consistent backups for disaster recovery.
The version-control system must run on every hardware platform and operating system in your architecture, or the systems it cannot reach will not adopt version control.
Choose version control with branching and tagging able to snapshot and repeat a tree state; tagging is vital for production change control.

Structure the repository as /trunk (mainline development), /production (tested production-ready code), and /tags (push-ready snapshots), and leverage version control for deployment, not only development.
Use version control religiously in production troubleshooting: it provides concise history of what changed, when, and why, and enables reverting via a stable tag or backing out a single changeset.
Bare-metal recovery cannot be replaced, but many disastrous failures (wrong IPs after a reboot, a missing config file, a missing cron job) do not require it.
The more aggressive the production push schedule, the more oddities arise in the production environment.
condition: aggressive or frequent production pushes

statement: Track and document emergency, ad-hoc production configuration changes in version control — for example, rsync /etc and key config directories to a control box and commit them, or place files directly under version control on each host.
Understanding how a server's configuration changed over time is more valuable than restoring it to a point in time, because it reveals the cause and effect of changes.
No amount of planning or procedure compensates for a poorly designed architecture, which fails under stress and lacks the infrastructure for real-time analysis and modification.
Prove a technology is the right fit before adopting it as a building block in a large architecture.
Design the system first and hold coders to an architecturally savvy standard — think like an architect who sees the whole system, not just a coder.
Regular collaboration among the business, development, and operations teams is the most fundamental ingredient of good ongoing design.
The five key aspects of a mission-critical environment are high availability, monitoring, software management, avoiding overcomplication, and optimization.
The criticality of an environment has nothing to do with its scale: high availability concerns resilience to failure, while load balancing concerns scale.
100% uptime is impossible; five-nines availability (99.999%) permits only about 5.26 minutes of downtime per year.
Define high availability as the absence of unplanned outages; scheduled maintenance windows are responsible and reduce the risk of unexpected outages.
Do not blindly trust that a high-availability solution is working — monitor the architecture top to bottom so failed pieces are caught early before their effects propagate.
Bottom-up (systems) monitoring is necessary but incomplete; pair it with top-down (business-level) monitoring, because what ultimately matters is that the business is running.
Monitoring must evolve hand-in-hand with architecture, application, and business changes; stale monitoring (watching obsolete things, missing new metrics) creates a dangerous false sense of security.
SNMP is the de-facto monitoring protocol — most commercial components ship SNMP agents — but many free and open-source tools, notably mail transport agents, do not.

For a component that does not expose a needed metric over SNMP, either fetch it via a simpler channel such as SSH or HTTP, or export it over SNMP (efficient and integrable, but with high authoring overhead).
A capable monitoring system must support notifications with automatic escalation when a failure is not resolved within a set time.
Encode service-dependency relationships into notification logic so a root-cause failure suppresses redundant downstream alerts (do not alert a time skew on a server that has crashed).

Support maintenance windows (monitor but suppress escalation) and event acknowledgment (suspend notifications safely) instead of manually disabling monitors, and poll expensive or slow-changing metrics less frequently than cheap or volatile ones.
Monitor a distributed service by exercising the service to perform a representative task and checking the result, rather than monitoring a single daemon's health.
A production environment has three vital tiers: development, staging, and production.
Make the staging environment as close to production as possible — ideally an exact replica down to hardware and software versions — because complex systems fail in unexpected ways.
When staging and production are identical, avoid pushes: once a release is staged, tested, and approved, point production traffic at the staging environment and swap their roles.
The best technical solution is not always the right business solution; infrastructure decisions are cost-benefit trade-offs to maximize return on investment.

On a roughly $1M-production versus $10k-dev/staging architecture, about 1 in 5 pushes had a mild negative impact and about 1 in 500 failed catastrophically, yet a full staging environment would have cost $2–3M more — exceeding the cost of those mistakes.
exception: the calculus is business-specific; a bank should not accept this risk

statement: Apply emergency releases (a security exploit or a crippling acute bug) with extreme haste but as safely as possible.
A good architect constantly fights to keep the architecture simple (KISS); minimizing the required infrastructure and its maintenance cost is part of being cost-effective.
Complex systems are harder to operate, develop, extend, and troubleshoot, and they tend to grow even more complex each time they are modified.
Scalability means a system can grow and shrink without fundamental change; performance and scalability are orthogonal properties.

Scrutinize and judge the performance of every architectural component you introduce, because a single slow or non-scaling component damages the scalability of the whole architecture and can capsize it.
Speeding up code inside a bottleneck has a far larger impact than speeding up code outside it (Amdahl), reinforced by the 90/10 rule that 90% of execution time is spent in 10% of the code.

Optimize the most common execution path, not the slowest component: a 50% speedup of code that runs 0.1% of the time yields only 0.05% overall, while a 50% speedup of code that runs 5% of the time yields a significant 2.5%.

Make performance review and tuning a perpetual cycle with all code open to revision, and regularly zoom out from microscopic to macroscopic analysis — reframing the question (for example, why do these log files exist, or why is this in a database) finds better solutions.

Never entrust a mission-critical architecture to a single person: personnel are part of the architecture, and one indispensable operator reintroduces a single point of failure into a no-single-point-of-failure system.

Fault tolerance is the capability of a system or component to continue normal operation despite hardware or software faults, and the number of faults it can withstand before normal operation is impaired.
A system is 1-fault-tolerant if it survives a single component failure and N-1-fault-tolerant if it survives all but one component failing (the strongest guarantee possible).
Hardware needed to carry routine load cannot be counted as redundant — if you rely on supposedly redundant hardware to handle normal load, it is not redundant at all.
SMTP has intrinsic fault tolerance (a mail transfer agent tries the listed mail exchanges in order of preference), whereas HTTP has none, so web high availability must be explicitly architected.
No enterprise-ready, horizontally scalable, N-1-fault-tolerant database system exists; the problem is expensive to solve correctly, so the accepted approach is to engineer around it.

Troubleshooting distributed systems is dramatically harder than single-node systems, because one conceptual web transaction is actually many short HTTP requests that may each arrive at a different cluster machine, obscuring cause and effect.
Unify logging across all machines in a cluster to recreate a single-instance view, so traditional cause-and-effect troubleshooting can be applied.

As availability demands rise the margin for error shrinks, so developers, system administrators, and DBAs must work more closely, and application programmers must handle content- and session-synchronization across the cluster.
Clearly define whether a system needs high availability, load balancing, or both before starting implementation.

High availability means remaining available despite the failure of components (above and beyond fault tolerant); load balancing means providing a service from multiple systems by distributing requests to combine their resources.

An optimal load-balanced system is impossible (it would require knowing all future requests and every machine's available resources), and most products are 'load distributors' rather than true 'load balancers.'
The goal is not to build an optimal system (impossible) but to run the business well — a system that meets business needs at a reasonable total cost of ownership.
Load balancing is not high availability: it relocates the failure problem to a different tier (shifting responsibility from system to network administrator) without adding any availability assurance.

High availability is not load balancing: HA implies nothing about efficient resource use or capacity (in hot-standby HA one node contributes 100% while others contribute 0%), and legitimate load balancing requires an intelligent resource-allocation mechanism.

A single hardware HA/load-balancing device is itself a single point of failure, so deploy two — but recognize the irony that the balancer then needs its own HA solution; and remember that vendors' selling points are not buying points, as some advertised advantages may not apply to your architecture.
High-availability failover relies on heartbeats; standard failover protocols include VRRP (IETF), Cisco's proprietary HSRP, and OpenBSD's CARP.
The core challenges of high availability are shared storage, application awareness of failures, and responsibility migration.
Web services rarely need shared storage because they are horizontally scalable and already run on every node; when shared storage is needed, NFS or NAS usually suffices.
The path-of-least-resistance approach to database high availability is shared attached storage plus a heartbeat between two machines.

Hardware HA/load-balancing devices make financial sense in front of hundreds or thousands of servers but little sense scaled down, and they force you to pay for load balancing even when you need only high availability.
Just because a solution will work does not mean it is the right tool for the job; match the solution to whether the business needs are stable or dynamic.
Traditional pairwise hot-standby failover leaves one machine completely idle, wasting its capacity.
A cluster is a set of like machines providing a particular service, united to increase robustness and/or performance and working in unison toward a goal.

In peer-based high availability the cluster as a whole — not any specific machine — owns a set of services and IP addresses, and each available machine negotiates to assume a subset; which machine holds which IP is irrelevant as long as at least one machine survives.

Chaining master-slave so that every machine is master of one service and slave of another, in order to keep multiple machines active, is overly complicated and failure-prone; peer-based high availability is the better answer.

Peer-based high availability runs the failover logic on the service machines themselves, avoiding both dedicated failover hardware and a new front-end device that would add monitoring, maintenance, upgrade complexity, and specialized skills.

Every new component adds cost — new monitoring, more maintenance, more complex upgrades, specialized skills, and harder, costlier troubleshooting — so never underestimate the obscure problems a new component introduces into a complex system.
Pure peer-based high availability needs multiple IP addresses to use more than one machine simultaneously, which clashes with IP-unfriendly services such as SSL.

Because the SSL certificate is handed to the client before it can request a specific one and its common name must match the host, a single IP can serve at most one SSL common name — so 1,000 SSL sites need at least 1,000 IP addresses, whereas plain HTTP serves unlimited named sites per IP.

For peer-based high availability with more than one active machine, each machine must provide the service authoritatively and tolerate concurrent use without malfunction — DNS and web services fit well, while databases pose tremendous challenges.
condition: more than one machine is active concurrently

statement: Services unsuited to multi-IP peer high availability still benefit from N-way hot-standby — many databases work with a single active node, electing or choosing a new master for the single advertised IP on failure.
High availability applies beyond the web, and the most commonly ignored fault-tolerance gap is networking equipment — firewalls, switches, and routers.

The reliability of network equipment breeds neglect — a switch may run a year with zero administration, fostering the false belief it needs no maintenance, yet plugging in another device can leave it no longer optimally configured.

System administrators should learn enough network engineering to recognize when they need review or assistance, because a single switch acting as a single point of failure can negate all their other work.

Commodity Intel servers running Linux or FreeBSD can serve as routers (multicast, IPSEC, tunneling, VoIP, full routing protocols) for around $1,000, and the only real remaining vendor argument against them — high availability — is answered by free VRRP and peer-based high availability.
Load balancing does not mean balancing the system load average (run-queue length over 1, 5, and 15 minutes); that metric is the wrong basis for web load balancing.
Web work is very short (milliseconds), so a freshly added server reads a load of 0 and would attract all requests, and the metric updates too slowly to drive sound decisions — the staleness problem.
Base load balancing on the effective utilization of available resources, not on total resources or system load.
Round-robin load balancing gives each server one request in rotation but never lets an overworked server recover, a classic queueing-theory problem.
Least-connections load balancing is relatively sound but breaks down when several load balancers make decisions in parallel.

Combine random allocation with resource-based algorithms as a probabilistically strong answer to the staleness problem; purely weighted-random balancing needs constant manual re-tweaking on every server add or upgrade.
Parallel or peer load balancers must cooperate — uncooperative balancers making the same decision double the intended effect, so a random distribution can beat the smartest uncooperative algorithm.
No single load-balancing model applies equally well to all practical situations.
Two machines cannot share one IP address on the same Ethernet segment because of ARP, so without a virtual-IP load-balancing device the rule is at least one distinct IP address per machine.
DNS can expose multiple IP addresses per hostname (round-robin DNS) but guarantees no even distribution; in practice a naive, unintelligent uniform distribution emerges only over long time spans.
SSL/HTTPS prevents name-based virtual hosting because the cryptographic handshake completes before the HTTP Host header is sent, so multiple secure sites cannot share a single IP address.
Do not work around SSL IP consumption by running SSL on a non-default port — many corporate firewalls allow SSL only on port 443, causing accessibility problems that are not easily rectified.

A delegate-namespace workaround (such as secure.example.com) saves IP addresses but diminishes user trust when the browser's URL or host visibly changes mid-transaction; run each secure site on at most one IP to alleviate, not fix, the problem.

Web switches (black-box load balancers) are the most popular technology for scaling high-traffic sites and are sometimes the only viable option given their raw performance (up to ~15M concurrent sessions and 50+ Gbit/s).
IP virtual servers (IPVS) serve the same purpose as web switches but run as software on commodity servers and are topologically identical to a web-switch deployment.

Application-layer (user-space) load balancers add features web switches lack — allocating on encrypted SSL-session content, routing pipelined HTTP requests to different servers, and business-rule allocation — but at far lower performance than layer-4/7 switches.

Operating at layer 3 lets a load balancer avoid application-protocol knowledge, enabling hardware acceleration (orders of magnitude faster) and versatility across SMTP, POP3, IMAP, DNS, FTP, and NNTP.
Packet translation manipulates packets (possible at immense scale) whereas proxying processes all client and server data and reforms packets, which is substantially more expensive.
Requirements, not convenience, dictate the load-balancing solution — if a web switch or IPVS cannot meet a functional need, it is eliminated entirely, not merely deprioritized.

Linear scaling is a falsehood: doubling machines cannot double capacity because optimal allocation needs future knowledge, so horizontal scaling is sublinear and per-server utilization falls as machines are added.
For capacity planning, expect about 70% per-server utilization on clusters of three or more nodes (HPC reaches ~95% with a steady stream of long jobs, but short web requests do worse).

Design load balancers as a resource-allocation framework so the architect can choose the allocation approach and plug in better algorithms or intelligent segmentation such as per-customer-tier routing.

Load balancing does not provide high availability — a single load balancer is a single point of failure, so two plus an HA solution between them are required; decentralizing across N sites multiplies this cost (four sites need eight load balancers), at which point alternatives may be more appropriate.
Session stickiness is not load balancing — routing a visitor to a fixed machine on information other than load metrics is not balancing load.
Storing session state only on the local app or web server necessitates sticky sessions and creates a single point of failure, because that user's session is lost if the server dies.

Split session data — keep rarely accessed or updated parts in a central backing store and frequently accessed or updated parts in the client's cookie — to remove sticky sessions and radically improve load balancing.
Storing sessions in shared storage such as a database is common but can require tremendous horsepower.
Most content, by volume and by count, is static, and dynamic-content serving techniques are inefficient when applied to static content.
Letting images trickle in is not a real fix for inefficient static serving — the user has not seen the intended page until its images load (it only mitigates for slow dial-up connections).

Establish specific performance goals before optimizing — for example model the peak (3M visitors/day, 15% in the peak hour, 5 pages each) to derive ~125 initial and ~500 subsequent page loads per second.
Model initial and subsequent page loads separately, because the browser cache holds images locally and avoids reloading them on later pages.
A single page load opens multiple TCP connections (for example seven, open about four seconds on average), most induced by page dependencies rather than the base document.
Apache 1.3 dedicates one process per connection for that connection's entire life, including all lag, pauses, and slow delivery, which is wasteful when serving slow clients.
On a heavily loaded web server, unlike a workstation, nearly all processes are simultaneously on the CPU or waiting on an in-demand resource, so context-switching cost becomes significant.

Serving a web request takes far more than two context switches: each network or disk interaction forces a switch out and back, so the bare minimum (accept, read, write, log, close) is about ten (around six amortized over a persistent connection), and real I/O makes ten a rarely-achieved lower bound.

Context switching is not free: at roughly 10 microseconds per switch a server does about 100,000 switches per second, so 10,000 requests/second at ten switches each would consume 100% of CPU just switching — budget for it (about 10% of CPU at 1,000 requests/second).
Alternative web-server models (thread-per-request, event-driven, or in-kernel serving) reduce context-switching cost versus the process-per-connection model.
Apache 1.3.x's process-limit problems often must be solved without switching platforms, because of its stability, flexibility, and wide adoption.

Serve static content with a lightweight, single-purpose server rather than a heavyweight dynamic one: heavyweight Apache processes (mod_perl or mod_php) use over 20MB each while barebones static processes use under 1MB, so the same 2GB box runs fewer than 100 dynamic but thousands of static processes.
Small, low-traffic sites can serve all content from one general-purpose server, but large multi-server sites hit resource shortages and must segregate serving by content type.

Serving static content from heavyweight dynamic servers wastes enormous capacity — for example about 3.58 visits/second versus about 100 visits/second when the dynamic server serves only dynamic content.

The real goal of a static-serving architecture is to serve peak traffic cost-effectively (fewest resources per visit) so the same hardware serves far more visitors and scales up and down more cheaply; accelerating the user experience is only a secondary side effect.
Segregate static from dynamic content so each can be scaled orthogonally — design to allow this, not to require it.

Support content segregation from within the application by generating static URLs through a single configurable helper function pointing at a base domain, never by hardcoding absolute URLs, so you can switch domains or CDNs or revert by changing one value.
A priori placement means hosting files on each node before they can be served, a problem greatly simplified for cacheable static content.

Static-content distribution is simpler than dynamic-code distribution because you already forfeit control (allowing remote caching) and add or remove objects rather than change them in place (in-place change is unreliable), so no complex clusterwide consistency semantics are needed.
Keep dynamic code consistent across all nodes — running new code on one node and old code on another invites disaster, especially when a user's sequential requests are serviced by different nodes.
Align the static- and dynamic-content distribution mechanisms to reduce confusion, because different policies or pitfalls for each invite human mistakes.

rsync (differential synchronization) is network-efficient but trades network for local CPU by checksumming files on already-busy servers, and a single master bears N times the cost for N nodes — no good network- and resource-efficient 1-to-N distribution tool exists.

NFS centralizes one content copy but is a single point of failure (clients cannot operate without the file server) and is weak over a WAN; AFS and CODA cache locally and are WAN-friendlier but still struggle when disconnected.

Cache-on-demand deploys a reverse-proxy web cache (a 'web accelerator' such as Apache mod_proxy or Squid) in front of the site; it fetches from the authoritative origin only on a cache miss, then serves subsequent requests from cache.

A reverse-proxy cache offloads the origin two ways: it serves previously seen content from cache, and it absorbs expensive client TCP handling so the origin talks only over low-latency, high-throughput links while the cache spoon-feeds slow clients.
Cache-on-demand is inherently less efficient than direct serving (extra work for misses and freshness checks), so benchmark whether the degradation is acceptable.

Benchmark candidate platforms on your own hardware and workload before choosing, because measured throughput directly sets machine count (for example ~800 req/s for Apache versus ~3,500 for thttpd versus ~2,800 for Squid yields 20 versus 5 versus 6 servers at 70% capacity).
For single-purpose work, prefer a simple, single-purposed, efficient server over a flexible, complex, multipurpose one that allocates more resources per connection.
A smaller cluster is better beyond hardware cost: it is easier and cheaper to manage and simpler to troubleshoot.
Do not choose a heavyweight platform for features you will not use; match the platform to the actual job.
The static-content tier must meet the same or stricter availability requirements as the dynamic tier, because it is a necessary part of the overall service.
Size for peak with spare capacity for surges and failures — for example keep six servers when four meet peak, making the tier two-fault tolerant.
Distribute requests with multiple round-robin DNS A records plus peer-based high availability (such as Wackamole) for IP availability, avoiding a dedicated load-balancer device.

The specific Unix-like OS rarely matters; choose by practical factors — community support for your key software on that platform, well-tested support for your HA tool, and event-system support (for example Squid with kqueue on FreeBSD gives higher concurrency at lower CPU).
Restrict each host's firewall to only the traffic it needs (for example inbound 80 and 22, outbound DNS on 53, and the Spread ports).
Wackamole drives a deterministic IP-assignment algorithm over a cluster via Spread group-communication semantics, supporting both active-passive and all-active multi-machine configurations.

Choose peer-based high availability over an HA/load-balancing device when scaling horizontally or geographically: where you already own an HA/LB device at one site, reuse it, but replicating two devices per site across many sites becomes costly, making peer-based HA more cost-effective as you grow.
In peer-based high availability, do not artificially prefer which machine holds which IP address — let the cluster collectively decide.
On IP failover within a subnet, the new owner must send unsolicited (gratuitous) ARP to refresh neighbors' and the router's ARP caches, or traffic keeps flowing to the dead machine's MAC address.

Test high availability by actually killing a node (pull the power), not just inspecting local config, because the router's ARP cache is the real test — and beware devices (such as the Cisco PIX firewall) that block ARP spoofing and break gratuitous-ARP failover.
Use a maturity delay before a newly joined cluster member assumes responsibility for virtual interfaces, to reduce flapping.
Round-robin DNS distribution is uneven second-to-second (around 30% deviation between servers) but stabilizes over minutes (under 3% deviation) — sufficient though not perfectly balanced.

Place content servers close to users on the network to cut latency and raise throughput by avoiding congested networks, because idle TCP latency is the second-largest waste of resources after low bandwidth.
Do not route users to a regional cluster by guessing their geographic location (asking the user or geo-locating their IP), because both methods are highly inaccurate.
Optimize for the user's proximity on the network, not their geographic location — what matters is where the user is on the Internet, not literally in the world.

DNS round-trip-time steering lets local resolvers converge on the lowest-latency authoritative server with no special infrastructure, but it suffers convergence delay (misdirection until converged) and breaks on network-topology changes.
Anycast gives multiple servers the same IP address and announces its routes so packets follow the shortest network path to the nearest instance.

Anycast breaks TCP — a mid-session route change delivers packets to a different host that aborts the unknown session with a RST — so use Anycast for connectionless UDP services such as DNS, not for TCP.

Combine Anycast DNS with unique per-node IPs: Anycast the DNS servers, each returning its local cluster's IP addresses, so a client's query is answered by the nearest DNS server and directed to the nearest cluster.

A globally distributed CDN of self-contained per-site clusters (commodity servers plus Wackamole IP failover plus a Squid cache-on-demand tier plus Anycast DNS) needs no out-of-band content synchronization and scales geographically without core change.
Caching dynamic content is harder than static content because the data changes over time and can differ from one viewer to another.
A computer cache is only an optimization — a cache miss costs only time, never correctness — so a cache may be purged at will or be missing when convenient.

Aim for high horizontal-scaling efficiency: no matter how fast the application is, it is capped if it cannot scale horizontally, and if doubling the hardware yields only a few percent more capacity the architecture is broken.
There are five basic caching approaches, each with its place, and a given approach is sometimes impossible given the nature of the underlying data.

A transparent (layered) cache is a proxy in front of the architecture that serves from a private cache and repopulates on a miss from the authoritative source; it is ideal for static content because a commodity proxy can hold the whole store for a near-100% hit rate.
Transparent caching deploys in front of web servers with no configuration changes (as a bridge or IP gateway) and is invisible to clients.
Use an accelerating proxy cache to spoon-feed slow clients, so the expensive application server completes its work over a fast local link and proceeds to the next job.
Application servers cost more than static servers because they construct content (more RAM and CPU), so do not waste them spoon-feeding slow clients — front them with an accelerating proxy cache.
An accelerating proxy is often worth deploying for its spoon-feeding benefit alone, even when the page content is unique and the cache hit rate is near zero.
An integrated (look-aside) cache is built into the application: it stores the results of expensive operations and answers from local data instead of requerying the authoritative source.
Apply computational reuse — store a computation's result when re-finding it is cheaper than recomputing it (a memoized Fibonacci dropped from about 6.1 seconds to under 0.01 seconds).
Computational reuse yields a performance gain, not scalability; high performance does not ensure scalability, but low performance is a death warrant.
Computational reuse assumes the answer never changes; for data that can change, add a cache-invalidation system or a time-to-live that accepts a bounded staleness margin.

Recursive DNS caching works because every datum ships with an explicit time-to-live; web-application queries usually lack an explicit TTL (the implicit one is the request's life), so design cacheable data to carry an explicit TTL.

The intrinsic problem with application-level integrated caching is that the cache is distributed and uncoordinated — a node that caches a query result cannot know when the underlying data changed; only the database knows.

Prefer a database-level data cache (such as MySQL's query cache) over application-level integrated caching where possible, because one product controls both the cache and the authoritative data and can efficiently invalidate answers when their underlying data changes.
Most Internet data has a high read-to-write ratio (read far more often than written), which is what makes caching and read replicas effective.

A write-back cache performs all modifications on the cache and writes to the backing store lazily on eviction; it risks corruption and data loss on power failure, so it suits non-durable data or needs battery-backed storage and does not adapt well to distributed web systems.

Use a write-thru cache — write to both the cache and the backing store — exploiting that reads often follow recent writes (the newest news is read most), so freshly written data is pre-cached for the likely reads.

A collaborative distributed cache makes one node's stored result benefit all nodes — it becomes 'the' cache, not 'its' cache — and because the data lives on the nodes that use it, a single failure does not threaten availability.

A one-to-many single-writer replicated cache (such as stock quotes from one feed) is the easy case; a multi-writer distributed cache (such as an SSL session cache published from all nodes) is far harder because network partitions and merges arise.

Cache SSL session state in a distributed cache so any machine can serve a returning client without a fresh expensive asymmetric handshake, instead of stickily pinning the client to its original, possibly overloaded, server.
Deploying a cache has two parts: choose the right technology (or mix of technologies) for the data, then place it in the architecture.

A cache is not required for operation, only for performance and scalability, so the architecture can revert to running without it; once an efficient low-operational-cost cache is deployed, do not remove it unless replacing it with something better.
The goal of caching is scalability — reducing contention on shared resources — not merely performance; the speedup is a by-product.
Contention on a shared, non-horizontally-scalable resource (such as a central database) is the enemy of horizontal scalability, because as the web tier scales out the stress on that resource rises.
When analyzing scalability, measure the portion of each request spent on non-scalable shared resources (such as database time), not just total response time, because only that portion limits scaling.

The architectural goal is to eliminate or minimize shared-resource usage per request, leaving the parallelizable, horizontally scalable work; tuning the database itself is a separate performance concern for the DBA.

Choose cache semantics up front: time-to-live caching is 'easy and incorrect' (it accepts a staleness margin) while explicit invalidation is 'complicated and correct' — pick by your tolerance for stale data.
For high read-to-write data, time-to-live caching wastes most purges: the TTL must be set low enough to surface rare updates, discarding still-valid data on every cycle.

When you control the write path (publishing), prefer caching indefinitely and invalidating explicitly on change over short time-to-live values, to capture the full benefit of a high read-to-write ratio.
Wrap expensive data accessors in cache get/set wrappers (check the cache, compute on a miss, store the result) to add caching with minimal code change.

memcached is a distributed, non-replicated cache: items cached on one node are visible to others, and a node crash deterministically fails over, with the lost partition treated as a premature purge causing no harm.
Segment memcached clusters administratively to control how many nodes each cache spans — useful when clusters are separated by an expensive network link or when there are too many concurrent clients.
A non-replicated distributed cache like memcached has only a 1/N chance the item is local, so as the cluster grows lookups increasingly hit remote machines — cheaper than the database, but not free.

Replicate frequently read, rarely changing data (such as article content with a near-100% hit rate) to every node so reads are local; because a cache need not be atomic or durable, replication can be lazy under an 'if in doubt, purge' policy.

Active replication propagates cache operations (add/get/delete) as they happen; passive replication stores remotely fetched items locally (cache-on-demand for caches) and suits TTL caches, but explicit-invalidation caches still need active delete and update propagation for consistency.
Simple lazy cache replication is acceptable only when operations need not be atomic; if you need atomic cache operations you are using the wrong tool and should use a replicated database.

Cache per-user data (preferences and session) in the user's own cookie — a multi-million-node, user-centric, wildly scalable cache that avoids spending server cache resources on data used in short bursts days apart.

Split session data: keep frequently or recently used parts in the cookie and rarely used parts in a central backing store; the author has never encountered an architecture where this split was impossible.
Server-side caches such as memcached give per-user data a poor hit rate (around 80%), because each user's data is unique and the finite cache evicts it between the user's infrequent visits.

Secure cookie-stored data with symmetric encryption (such as AES) for confidentiality plus a message digest (such as SHA-1) for integrity, which defeats the common objections to storing data in cookies.
Defend against theft of valid cookies by embedding and refreshing a timestamp on each validated request, rejecting cookies whose timestamp is too old and forcing re-authentication.
Separate page content into a slowly changing shared part (the same for everyone) and a per-viewer dynamic part, because transparent whole-page caching fails when only part of the page is cacheable.

Use two-tier execution: run the page once to render the slowly changing content into an intermediate cached template, then execute that template per request for the per-viewer content, pushing stable data all the way out to the web server so neither the database nor a remote cache is touched.

Script compilation is distributed and shared-resource-free, so compiler caches are only a performance optimization (already solved for popular languages), whereas execution that pulls from shared resources is the real scalability cost to avoid.

Invalidate file-based compiled caches by deleting the files across all nodes; if a node is down during invalidation, blow its cache before it rejoins the cluster rather than building complex synchronization.
The key to successful caching is understanding the true nature of your data — how frequently it changes and where it is used.

Distributed-database technologies solve distinct problems — data resiliency, operational failover, increased query performance, complete reliability, and geographically distributed operation — that must not be conflated.

Data resiliency keeps a complete, consistent, current copy of data elsewhere against disaster or hardware failure by shipping modifications in near real-time; operational failover adds a production-grade standby that can assume operations (warm-standby is manual, hot-standby is automatic).
Use read-only replicas (slave databases that never become master) to scale read-heavy workloads, since most architectures have a high read-to-write ratio.

Near-real-time asynchronous replication is not complete reliability — transactions committed just before a failure may never reach the standby — so for nonstop reliability a transaction must not commit until a peer agrees to commit it, trading speed for safety.

Replication is hard because of ACID: the single-host techniques that enforce atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability cheaply (shared memory, local synchronization, a shared buffer cache) do not generalize across a network without large performance and availability costs.

Distributed ACID is dominated by atomicity (all nodes commit or all abort), consistency (a consistent global ordering of commits across nodes), and durability (cluster-wide agreement on committed state); isolation is largely unaffected by distribution.

Tripling a multimaster cluster does not triple transactional throughput — read-only queries can scale almost linearly, but total transactional throughput falls when transactions touch the same data; near-linear gain occurs only for disjoint data aggregation.

Two-phase commit safely coordinates distributed commits and is the only common correct multimaster technique, but its lock-step progress halts on a single down node and demands resynchronization, making it ill-suited to wide-area replication over hostile networks.
Group-communication techniques such as extended virtual synchrony (EVS) help multimaster replication survive disconnected networks and partitions that bare two-phase commit cannot.

On a network partition, multimaster replication has only two options — manual intervention (an operator redefines the consensus set, then resynchronizes excluded nodes) or quorums — because no unanimous commit vote can form across the split.

A quorum is an improper subset of the group permitted to make a decision; a correct quorum algorithm guarantees that at most one quorum exists at any time regardless of node count, the simplest being a majority.

Use a quorum algorithm to guarantee replication progress through arbitrary network partitions and merges, and tune it to business priorities (for example weight a corporate-HQ node, or require five of six nodes, or any two nodes if one is HQ).

Extended virtual synchrony provides reliable, ordered group messaging without two-phase commit's cost — a delivered message guarantees that all recipients saw the same group membership at delivery — which is what makes distributed ACID replication provable.
Multimaster replication is not ready for most environments because people want it for both increased availability and increased performance, and you cannot have both.

Master-master replication (exactly two nodes over a low-latency interconnect) makes two-phase-commit overhead reasonable, so 2PC is how two-node replication is done — but it adds availability, not scalability.

Master-slave replication solves a different problem than multimaster and gives weaker availability and fault-tolerance guarantees, but treat that difference as a different tool for a different job, not a weakness.
In master-slave replication, data is modified only at the master while slaves serve read-only queries, scaling read-intensive performance almost linearly and sometimes super-linearly.
There are two master-slave methods: operation (DML) replication ships the statement for each slave to re-plan and execute, while changeset (DML-log) replication ships the actual changed rows.

The operation-versus-changeset choice only matters for two DML classes: expensive-DML-with-small-change favors changeset (avoid recomputing on every slave), and cheap-DML-with-large-change favors operation (avoid shipping millions of rows); the other two classes are a wash.
Massive data changes and expensive queries that yield tiny results should both be rare in production OLTP — if many of your queries fall in those classes, revisit your queries and data model.
Changeset replication tends to be more reliable and adapts more easily to cross-vendor replication (such as Oracle to PostgreSQL or MySQL).
On a LAN, network and I/O bandwidth are cheaper than CPU and memory, favoring changeset replication; on a WAN, network can cost more, favoring operation replication.

For horizontal scale, master-master cannot add nodes and multimaster two-phase commit collapses at scale (a 100-node config means each node runs 2PC with 99 peers), so master-slave is the only replication approach that scales horizontally.

Per-processor database licensing (such as Oracle's) favors vertical scaling, so for a horizontally scaled read tier use cheaper replicas (such as PostgreSQL) around the existing core rather than licensing the master database on every node.
Do not change what works if you can help it — keep the proven core database and add cheaper replicas around it, leveraging existing developer expertise (PostgreSQL is closer to Oracle than MySQL is).
Generic cross-vendor master-slave replication, implemented in an application external to the source and destination databases, lets you genuinely pick the right database tool for each task.

Track database changes with INSERT/DELETE/UPDATE triggers that record the changed primary key, transaction ID, and timestamp into a DML-log table; for a most-recent-view replica you need only the primary key of changed rows, not every intermediate value.
