Replay replication by transaction ID, not by timestamp: in databases 'since' means since-commit, not since-occurrence, so a timestamp high-water mark causes a race condition and inconsistent slaves.
Track each node's processed transaction IDs so every slave can determine which transactions are new on its next run.
A generic apply routine handles three cases by comparing the reference and new primary keys: a NULL new key means delete, an existing key means update, and an absent key means insert.

The slave replication loop is: connect to the master, request unprocessed modifications, apply them, inform the master, commit on both sides, and repeat on an interval — seeded once by exporting and importing the table.
DML-log and processed-transaction tables grow unbounded, so schedule periodic automated cleanup of their old records.
For small, infrequently changed tables, skip change-tracking and use snapshot replication — truncate, pull, insert, commit.
Avoid truncate-and-reload blocking read queries by using flipping snapshots: keep two copies plus a view, populate the inactive copy, then repoint the view.
Use the database's bulk-load facility (Oracle sqlldr, PostgreSQL COPY, MySQL LOAD DATA INFILE) or dblinks for bulk data movement rather than row-by-row inserts.

Limit the number of distinct products in an architecture — fewer products means less staff expertise required and fewer release and life cycles to track — and use the same product for the same job unless the new demand genuinely differs.

Before adding a different-vendor database, ask why the current database does not serve the new purpose, what specific missing features another product has, and whether the problem could be solved without a database at all.
Logging infrastructure is crucial for monitoring, auditing, and troubleshooting, yet it is one of the most neglected components of large architectures.
Logging is hard for two reasons — volume (a large site can generate ~17,000 log lines per second, about 360 million events per day) and aggregation across many sources (20+ servers).
For quantized aggregate reports, time-stamp accuracy is not critical: a time skew much smaller than the report's granularity (seconds versus hourly buckets) does not change the trends.
For distributed-system troubleshooting, relative time-stamp accuracy is paramount — events that comprise a transaction must be logged clusterwide in the order they occurred, which is a hard problem.

Batch (periodic pull) log aggregation is simple but flawed: a crash loses logs journaled since the last fetch, retroactively merging them silently changes already-computed historical statistics, and it precludes real-time analysis.

Real-time unicast push aggregation (such as Syslog) removes batch latency and enables real-time metrics, but naive Syslog over UDP is unreliable, so use a reliable TCP-based transport (Syslog-NG, mod_log_mysql).
Push log aggregation requires reconfiguring every publisher to add a redundant log host, because publishers must know where to push.

Passive sniffing aggregation manufactures logs from observed network traffic without reconfiguring publishers, but it requires a single egress monitoring point (rare in large or global topologies), cannot read SSL traffic, and silently drops logs under resource saturation — a bad idea when logs are vital.

Logging done right delivers all logs reliably in real-time, optionally to redundant servers, and turns the stream into operational business-level monitors (bounds on 500/404 rates, requests per second versus trend) that trigger immediately rather than from 24-hour roll-ups.
Support many log subscribers cheaply with reliable IP multicast (such as Spread), so adding subscribers does not require scaling up network infrastructure or bring the system to its knees.

Separate logging roles — web servers publish, log servers journal and retain, log monitors analyze and alert, casual monitors do ad-hoc inspection — so each role can have its own uptime, service level, and ownership.

A group-communication publish/subscribe substrate (such as Spread) makes log aggregation simpler and more elegant than batch, unicast, or sniffing approaches, needing only three components: a publication mechanism, a journaling subscriber, and the messaging substrate.
Keep the log-journaling component brain-dead simple (subscribe to groups, write messages to files), because simplicity makes it reliable and fast.

Do not let inertia or fear of code modification entrench the wrong technology — integrating a new approach is often an hour's work (such as a log4j-to-Spread bridge), and refusing it forfeits large advantages.
Routing logs through a publish/subscribe substrate instruments the whole architecture for performance assessment, debugging, monitoring, and auditing with little effort.

Build your own real-time web-cluster monitoring tools from the log stream, because web clusters lack the per-node real-time tooling (iostat, vmstat) that single systems have, and once the data is at your fingertips such tools are quick to write.
Log per-request service time, and per-statement database execution time, into the log stream so you can report average, minimum, and maximum latencies like iostat.

Keep your engineering-analytical thinking while taking a macroscopic business view: monitor technical business metrics (registrations, orders, click-through), because you uniquely see both technical and business metrics and the business reports already draw on your logs and databases.
Correlating business and technical metrics for a healthy system lets you recognize an unhealthy situation as it forms, using minute-level real-time trends.
Visualization is priceless for large datasets — graphs sharing a common time axis make cause-and-effect correlation across systems easy where raw numbers do not.
Set up metric collection before problems occur (as part of launching a service), not during troubleshooting, or you will have no historical baseline to compare against.

Choose the metric-collection interval from how long it takes to fully understand a graph (collect roughly twice that often); finer resolution is expensive and adds little, while multi-resolution retention (fine recent, coarse for years) covers history.
Metrics split into SNMP-queryable (easy — tools like Cacti auto-collect and auto-build the round-robin databases) and non-SNMP custom business metrics that need one-off collection scripts.
Maintain one-off custom collection scripts for non-SNMP business metrics — they are simple, similar to one another, and reusable across the organization.
Smuggle a custom field into an existing but unused log field (such as remote_user) so you add data without changing the log format or breaking existing parsers.

Define your metrics precisely and graph the right breakdown: a definition mismatch hid a problem (a 'hits up 2%' figure counted all log lines, not just 200 responses), and graphing by HTTP response code instantly exposed a 404 spike.
Centralized, remote logging gives a single audit portal and, critically, access to a misbehaving machine's logs even when the machine itself is unreachable.

Most development is feature design — adding to an already-designed application — which is the most common ground for mistakes; the core application should be designed once and well, since it is the basis for all later work.
Feature-design mistakes are smaller and easier to recover from than core redesign, but recognize bad design and refactor it, because death by pin pricks is a bad way to die.

Define the size and scope of the problem before building a solution — building first and sizing later wastes effort (a MySQL 'who's online' attempt reached only ~800 operations/second against a 9,000/second requirement).
Do not default to the tool that is already there (such as the site's RDBMS) merely because it is there; match the tool to the problem.

An RDBMS is the wrong tool when ACID is not needed — for a 30-minute 'who's online' view, durability, isolation, and multi-row consistency are irrelevant, so paying ACID's cost (full table scans, query-cache invalidation, sorts) is pure waste.

SELECT COUNT(*) and ORDER BY ... LIMIT can be far more expensive than they look: databases rarely keep accurate cardinality (so COUNT does real work), and a LIMITed top-N still fully sorts the resultset despite an index.

Never make a non-essential side task (such as view-tracking) synchronous with serving the request — if the side write slows, the whole site stalls; the right behavior is to serve slightly stale data while the back end catches up.

Process derived or auxiliary data passively from the already-flowing (free) log stream instead of synchronously in the request path, achieving near-real-time accuracy where the only failure mode under a surge is a small lag behind reality.
'Too slow' usually means 'inappropriate' — the tool is not necessarily slow, it is the wrong tool for the job.

For a hot in-memory lookup service, choose a platform that does not touch storage and whose data structures answer your exact questions cheaply (for example a purpose-built C service) rather than a general-purpose database.
Reuse infrastructure already privy to the needed data — a passive log subscriber that already receives all logs and supports loadable modules is a natural platform for a new log-driven service.

Do not be intimidated by bending tools to your will (poking a user ID into Apache's connection record, writing a PHP C extension to hook request shutdown); a working end-to-end prototype can take about an hour.
Use a compact binary protocol (length-prefixed fields in network byte order) for a fast internal service.
Eliminate expired data at maintenance time rather than at query time — pre-cull old entries (popping the oldest off a time-ordered index is O(1)) so queries never have to filter by age.

Choose data structures that answer your exact questions cheaply — for example a hash of URL counts plus a multi-indexed skiplist indexed exactly as the equivalent SQL (unique user ID, ordered hit-date, ordered URL-and-hit-date) — so an in-memory service mirrors the required access patterns.
Use C, or any language with cheap data management and granular control of data structures, for a performance-centric service that must sustain thousands of queries per second.
A non-blocking socket service must track partial-read progress per connection and resume when more data arrives (returning on EAGAIN).

Test against a dataset that fairly represents production, not arbitrary data; a passive, off-critical-path tracker can be tested on a fresh instance fed real production logs with almost no test-harness investment.
Warm the system up before measuring — a 30-minute activity window means realistic data exists only after 30 minutes of operation.

When performance is surprising, profile rather than guess: a 43 queries/second result was traced to Math::BigInt dominating, and passing the 64-bit ID as two 32-bit halves raised throughput to about 2,859 queries/second.

Test in the real deployment shape — run the client in parallel from many servers (eight nodes reached about 12,000 queries/second aggregate) — and aim for confidence rather than overengineering the test or chasing human-timing precision.

A service scales when it collects its information outside the critical service path (passive, log-stream-fed), so it can run on every web server without adding load to any other component — that, not raw per-box throughput, is the real testament to scalability.

Know your tools: understand the principles behind a tool's features to pick the right ones, weigh the cost of features you do not need (do not squash a mosquito with a cannon), and learn its quirks and caveats.

Use the group-communication paradigm for multi-party messaging where the participant set is small, identities matter, and members both send and receive; point-to-point among all participants is expensive and chaotic, while reliable IP-multicast fits a single sender broadcasting to many anonymous receivers.
A group-communication system provides group membership (the current member set plus join/leave notifications) and broadcast primitives characterized by reliability and ordering.
Message ordering guarantees are FIFO (per-sender order), causal (FIFO plus cross-sender happened-before), and total (all receivers see the same order).

Match the delivery guarantee to the need — the strongest guarantee (a SAFE/EVS delivery, given only once all daemons hold the message) is significantly slower than agreed or FIFO delivery, so do not use it casually.
Keep configuration identical across all nodes, because slightly different configs can leave daemons that appear healthy yet cannot communicate.

Use a publish-to-a-group messaging bus to decouple clients from servers: a client sends one message to the group and the bus reliably fans it out, so the client need not know or connect to each server individually (as in a distributed cache purge).

Match the consistency cost to the data's forgiveness — for cache-coherence purges, RELIABLE delivery suffices because a node that missed a purge (through a crash or partition) can simply clear its whole cache on restart and repopulate on demand, avoiding the expense of SAFE delivery and extra logic.

Diagnose messaging-substrate failures with raised debug verbosity, then revert; common failures are binding the wrong node name, a firewall blocking both the configured port and the port immediately above it, and multicast silently falling back to unicast (which then fails at three or more nodes).

Test application robustness against network faults by injecting artificial partitions (for example via spmonitor) and watch daemon health metrics (membership changes, retransmission counts) for signs of an unstable network.
